newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian steel sector seen in doldrums most of 1997.
newsitem.headline: Indian steel sector seen in doldrums most of 1997.

text.p: India's steel sector is likely to remain in the doldrums for most of 1997 because an increase in production capacity at home and abroad will keep sluggish steel prices in check, analysts said on Tuesday.
They said a slight rise in global hot-rolled coil (HRC) prices -- to the current $290 a tonne from $260 at the start of 1996 -- would not have a significant impact on domestic prices.
International steel prices were also unlikely to rise sharply in the coming year as new plants come on stream in the United States and Asia, they said.

"Indian steel prices could rise by a maximum four percent towards the end of February if the global rise continues, but that would not be enough to cover recent rises in administered prices," said Sandeep Neema, analyst at Kotak Securities, the Indian affiliate of Goldman Sachs.
Administered prices are government fixed prices for coal and diesel.
"All and all it looks like a difficult year ahead."
Steel companies have been reeling under rising prices for coal and petroleum products, such as diesel, in the 1996/97 (April-March) financial year.
Another blow to the industry was a cut in import duties announced in the annual budget in July.

"The new and enhanced flat-steel making capacity means that local producers cannot raise flat-steel prices even as global prices show signs of picking up," said analyst Rajeev Das at Paribas Capital Markets in Singapore.
In a review of the sector, Das said installed HRC capacity in India would rise to 15.3 million tonnes between the years 2000 and 2001, from 6.4 million tonnes in 1995/96.
He said domestic demand would not keep pace.

"From a level of 5.8 million tonnes in 1995-96, the demand for HRC should rise to 9.8 million tonnes in the year 2001, implying that Indian HRC manufacturers would need to export almost 5.5 million tonnes of HRC by that year," he said.
Analysts said a prolonged economic slowdown in the current financial year had seen demand slacken.

"Fresh capital investment decisions are being deferred, infrastructure projects are not being announced, the growth rate of several consumer goods has fallen -- the slowdown has had a major impact on the industry," said an analyst at securities firm James Capel B&K.
But some analysts said they had upgraded leading steel stocks because they were trading at cheap values.

"We are underweight on the sector but we have upgraded our stocks recommendations for some stocks after the way prices have fallen. These prices discount the poor earnings outlook for the sector," said analyst Anurag Mathur at Peregrine Capital.
Mathur said top Indian steel stocks Tata Iron and Steel Co (TISCO) and Steel Authority of India (SAIL) had been upgraded to "hold" from "sell".
